Vous êtes déclarés mari et femme

To form the passive voice: être (in any tense) + agreeing past participle.
To say who does the action, with “par” (or “de” with verbs of feeling).

To understand the official texts of a wedding.

Monday, 3 May, 11 a.m. The wedding room of the town hall of the 4th arrondissement. In the front row: Hélène, the grandmother with the mărțișor on her coat, Elena, Dan, Brigitte, Pierre. The deputy mayor begins the ceremony.
Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. The marriage of Mademoiselle Ioana Popescu and Monsieur Julien Moreau is celebrated today, in the presence of their families and friends.
First, I must read you a few articles of the Civil Code. “Spouses owe each other respect, fidelity, help and assistance.”
“Spouses together ensure the moral and material direction of the family.” These articles were written a long time ago, but they are still read at every wedding.
Monsieur Julien Moreau, do you take Mademoiselle Ioana Popescu as your wife?
Mademoiselle Ioana Popescu, do you take Monsieur Julien Moreau as your husband?
(in a trembling voice) Yes. Da. Yes!
(smiling) Both answers are accepted. In the name of the law, you are declared united by the bonds of marriage.
(he puts the ring on Ioana’s finger, next to the little green ring) With this ring, I promise you all my Thursdays, all my Mondays, and all my waltzes.
And I promise never to make you eat more than five sarmale a day.
(after the laughter) The witnesses are now invited to sign the register. Madame Hélène Morel, Monsieur Radu Popescu, Madame Odile Bernard, Monsieur Karim Haddad.
Here is your family record book. It is handed to you in the name of the Republic. And now, I believe a young musician has been invited to play for you…
(at the piano, very serious) This piece was composed in 1962 by Henri Bernard. It is played today for Hélène, for Ioana and for Julien.
has (“il y a longtemps” = a long time ago)
to make (“te faire manger” = to make you eat)
“Ee-la-ay-tay-kõ-po-zay”: three é’s in a row! Linked without a pause.
“Ay-poo” / “ay-pooz”: the s in the feminine “épouse” sounds like z.
“A-lee-ãs”: nasal -ance. The same word also means a political “alliance”.
“Kor-tezh”: in France, the procession of cars honks its horns on the way after the wedding.
“Lee-vreh duh fa-mee-y”: the official book received at the wedding, in which children are later recorded.

In the active, the subject does the action: “L’adjointe célèbre le mariage.” In the passive, the subject UNDERGOES the action: “Le mariage est célébré par l’adjointe.” Just like English: “The wedding is officiated by the deputy mayor.”
La valse a été composée par Henri.
Le piano sera joué par Julien.
The passive = the verb ÊTRE in the desired tense + the PAST PARTICIPLE of the verb, agreeing with the subject (like an adjective).
Les lettres étaient écrites à la main.
The letters were written by hand.
Les invités seront accueillis à midi.
The guests will be welcomed at noon.
In the passive, the participle ALWAYS agrees with the subject: “La valse a été composéE”, “Les témoins sont invitéS”, “Les alliances sont échangéES”.
The person who does the action (the agent) is usually introduced by PAR. After verbs of feeling and description, DE is used:
Madame Bernard is respected by her neighbours.
The room was decorated with flowers.
The agent can be left out when it isn’t important: “Les articles sont lus à chaque mariage.” (it doesn’t matter who reads them).
In everyday speech, French people often avoid the passive. They have two alternatives:
On ne dit pas ce mot.
Ce mot ne se dit pas.

Romanian does exactly the same with “se”: “se citesc”, “se vorbește”. English tends to use the passive or “people/you”: the French reflexive (“ça se dit”, “ça ne se fait pas”) is worth learning as fixed expressions.
5. Marriage at a French town hall

At every civil wedding in France, articles 212–215 of the Civil Code are read, about the rights and duties of spouses. On the way out, guests throw rice or petals, and the procession of cars honks its way through town.
The cake was made by Sophie.

Par qui le mariage est célébré ?
Qu’est-ce qui est lu à chaque mariage ?

All his Thursdays, Mondays and waltzes
This piece was composed in 1962 by Henri Bernard.

When the newlyweds came out of the town hall, they were greeted by a shower of rice and rose petals. Sophie had brought a whole basket of petals. Manon had put some in everyone’s hair, even in that of the old tailor Ferrand, who had been invited at the last minute.

On the steps, Ioana’s grandmother didn’t wait for the music. She took Pierre by the hand and made him dance a hora, right there, in front of the town hall, under the astonished eyes of passers-by. Pierre didn’t know the steps, but he was swept along by everyone.

Then the procession set off towards the Saône. As French tradition demands, all the cars were honking. Radu, who was driving the newlyweds’ car, honked louder than the others. He had been warned by Karim: “In France, a silent wedding brings bad luck!”

The restaurant had been chosen by Madame Bernard in November. It was an old house by the water, with a big terrace under the plane trees. The tables had been decorated with lily of the valley and little mărțișoare, made by the grandmother all winter.
The meal was served at two o’clock. There was Pierre’s bread, cheeses from Savoie, a Lyon dish… and, in the middle of each table, a dish of sarmale. Nobody asked where they came from. Everyone knew.

During the meal, speeches were made. Karim told how Ioana had arrived at the studio two years earlier, with a dictionary in her bag. Brigitte read a poem she had written herself, and cried before the end. Dan spoke in French, slowly, with a sheet of paper trembling in his hand.

“My daughter left for France alone,” he said. “We were afraid. Today she is surrounded by a family. Not a French family, not a Romanian family. A family. Thank you.” He couldn’t say any more. Elena took his hand.
Then Manon sang. Her voice had been trained for months with Julien, in secret. She sang an old French song, “La Vie en rose”. Even the waiters stopped to listen.

At about six o’clock, when the sun began to go down over the Saône, the pièce montée was brought in by Sophie and her husband. It was a tower of caramel cream puffs, as tall as a child. On top, instead of the usual little bride and groom, Sophie had placed a tiny sugar piano.

And then came the moment everyone had been waiting for. Julien stood up. On the terrace, an old piano had been set up by the restaurant, at Madame Bernard’s request. Julien sat down and looked at Hélène.
“This waltz,” he said, “was written sixty-five years ago, for a twenty-year-old girl. Today, that girl is eighty-five. Hélène, happy birthday.”

He began to play. Ioana crossed the terrace and held out her hand to Hélène. The old lady leaned her stick against the table. She stood up slowly, and they danced together, the bride in white silk and the girl from 1962.

At the second verse, Madame Bernard stood up in turn and invited the Romanian grandmother. Then Brigitte invited Elena. Then Dan invited Leïla, and Karim invited Nathalie, and Radu, as red as a tomato, invited Manon.

Soon the whole terrace was dancing Henri’s waltz, above the Saône as it turned orange. Only Julien wasn’t dancing. He was playing, and smiling, and thinking that a promise made in 1962 had finally just been kept.

When the music stopped, Hélène came back to the piano, out of breath and happy. She leaned towards Julien and whispered in his ear: “He would have been happy, you know. He would have been very, very happy.”

The party went on until midnight. The grandmother was the last to leave the dance floor. Karim’s cousin, who was the DJ, had been forced to look for Romanian music on his phone, because she refused to sit down before dancing one last hora.

When the newlyweds finally left, a big banner had been tied to their car by Radu and Manon. It said, in French and in Romanian: “Vive les mariés ! Trăiască mirii!” And underneath, in smaller letters, in Radu’s handwriting: “Caution, driver fed on sarmale.”

In the car, Ioana looked at her two rings: the little green stone and the brand-new wedding ring. “You know what’s strange?” she said. “I didn’t cry once today.” Julien laughed. “Ioana, you cried eleven times. I counted.”
would have (“il aurait été” = he would have been)

Un mariage pas comme les autres
Yesterday, Monday 3 May, a wedding unlike any other was celebrated at the town hall of the 4th arrondissement.
Ioana Popescu, a Romanian architect, and Julien Moreau, a music teacher, were married by the deputy mayor, in front of more than eighty guests.
The date wasn’t chosen by chance: it is the birthday of Madame Hélène Morel, eighty-five, the bride’s witness.
At the end of the ceremony, a waltz was played on the piano by Théo, twelve, a pupil of the groom. It had been composed in 1962 by a young man from Lyon for Madame Morel.
A grandmother who came from Romania by coach, after thirty hours on the road, was loudly applauded when she danced on the town hall steps.
The meal was served in a restaurant on the banks of the Saône. The bread had been made by the groom’s father, a baker in Annecy.
A second ceremony will be celebrated this summer in a village in Romanian Moldavia. All our best wishes for happiness to the newlyweds!
Pourquoi la date a été choisie ?
Par qui le pain a été fait ?
A second ceremony will be celebrated this summer.
